# Tutorial 1 — learning to multiply

**Read this one downwards.** Each section starts with a question, and the graph underneath
it is the answer. Hit Run once and everything below fills in; then pan down and follow it.

The problem is the smallest one that is still interesting: the network is given **two
numbers** and has to produce **their product**. Two in, one out. No images, no text, nothing
to download, about thirty seconds to train all six networks on this page.

By the bottom you will have watched a network fail at this twice, for two different reasons,
and you will be able to tell which reason from a picture rather than from a number.

**How to read the surface plots.** Every rung ends with three squares. The left one is the
answer the network *should* give for every pair of inputs — orange where the product is
positive, blue where it is negative. The middle one is what the network *does* give. The
right one is the difference. **When the middle square matches the left one, it has learned.
When the middle square is empty, it has not.**

## 1 · "I want a network that multiplies two numbers together."

Start with the thing working, so there is something to take apart.

Two numbers go in. A `Linear` layer turns them into sixteen intermediate numbers, a `Tanh`
bends each of those, and a second `Linear` collapses the sixteen back down to one. That
shape — **widen, bend, narrow** — is the majority of all neural networks ever built.

Look at the surface at the end of the row: the middle square matches the left one. It has
worked out multiplication from nothing but examples, to about four decimal places, using
**65 numbers** it tuned itself.

nodes.title: How to train, for all six
It matches. 65 numbers, learned from examples.

widgets_values:
## 2 · "Do I actually need the middle bit? Let me try the smallest thing first."

The honest first instinct. One `Linear` layer, straight from the two inputs to the one
output. Three numbers: a weight on `a`, a weight on `b`, and an offset.

**It fails completely.** Not badly — completely. It explains **0.0%** of the variation in
the answer, which is to say it does no better than ignoring the inputs and guessing the
average every time.

The middle square is *empty*. That emptiness is the finding: a `Linear` layer computes
`w₁a + w₂b + c`, and there is no choice of those three numbers that produces `a × b`. Not a
poor choice. No choice.

nodes.title: Empty. It explains 0.0% of the answer.

widgets_values:
## 3 · "Fine — it was too small. I will give it more parameters."

The obvious next move, and it is **wrong in an interesting way**.

This rung has two `Linear` layers and 65 numbers — the *same* count as the working network
in section 1, twenty-one times more than section 2. No activation between them.

**It also explains 0.0%.** Identical failure, twenty-one times the parameters.

Here is why, and it is worth holding on to: a linear function of a linear function is a
linear function. Stacking `Linear` layers with nothing between them collapses, algebraically,
into a single `Linear` layer. Those 65 numbers describe something that could be written with
3. **Depth without an activation is not depth at all** — it is an expensive way to write
section 2.

## 4 · "Does it have to be a Tanh, or will any bend do?"

Any bend will do. This is the same network as section 1 with `ReLU` in place of `Tanh` —
and `ReLU` is about as crude as a bend gets: it passes positives through untouched and flattens
everything negative to zero.

It works too — **99.9%**, against the `Tanh` network's 100%. Look closely at the right-hand
square and you can see *how* differently it got there: the `Tanh` network leaves a smooth,
rippled residue, while this one leaves **straight creases**, because it is assembling a
curved surface out of flat panels.

The lesson is that the activation's job is not to be any particular shape. Its job is to
**not be a straight line**, so that stacking layers stops collapsing.

nodes.title: Works too — but out of flat panels.

widgets_values:
## 5 · "How much of that width do I actually need?"

Sixteen intermediate numbers was a guess. This rung uses **two**, and gets **77.5%** of the
way there.

Look at *what* it did with them. The answer has four quadrants. Two `Tanh` units can only
bend the plane twice, so it built a **diagonal ridge** instead: it finds both positive
corners — where `a` and `b` share a sign — and then smears the two negative quadrants into a
single band, having run out of bends to separate them with.

This is what *not enough capacity* looks like, and it is worth learning by sight, because it
looks nothing like sections 2 and 3. Those were **empty**. This one is **wrong in a
structured way** — clearly it has learned something and been unable to finish.

An empty middle square means the network cannot express the answer at all, and more
parameters will not help. A middle square with the wrong shape in it means it can, and needs
more room. Those two failures look identical in a loss number.

nodes.title: Train — Only two in the middle
Close, and wrong at the edges.

widgets_values:
## 6 · "Was the network the problem, or was the problem the problem?"

Change the dataset node at the start of *this* row from `a × b` to `a + b`, and give it the
three-number network from section 2 — the one that failed completely.

**It is exact.** 100% of the answer, from three numbers.

Nothing about that network changed. It was never broken. Addition *is* a weighted sum of the
inputs, which is the literal definition of what a `Linear` layer computes, so the smallest
possible network is already the perfect tool for it.

That is the idea this whole tutorial exists to hand over: **a network is not good or bad, it
is matched or unmatched to the shape of the problem.** Section 2's network was the right
answer to a question nobody had asked yet. Everything that follows in this pack — the
convolutions, the attention, the skips — is somebody choosing a shape because the problem had
that shape first.
Three numbers, and that is enough
